THENGU: AMAZON BRAND STORE COPY (home page and 3 collection pages)

HOME PAGE

Hero line
Coconut skincare that stays light in Kerala's humidity.

Brand intro
Thengu is a Kochi skincare brand built around the coconut. We make creams, scrubs and washes for humid days, when a heavy product feels like too much. Our listings carry 4.3 stars from 1,860 Amazon ratings (as shown on 1 October 2026). Read what buyers say, then pick the collection that matches your skin.

Collection names (navigation)
Dry skin | Dull skin | Oily or sticky skin

Trust strip
4.3 stars, 1,860 ratings | 7-day returns, unopened packs | Pay on Delivery and UPI | Dispatched within 24 hours of order

What goes in
Every Thengu product is built around one named ingredient. Virgin coconut oil in the Rich Coconut Cream. Shea butter in the Coconut Body Butter. Turmeric in the Face Scrub. Coconut milk in the Face Wash. Aloe vera in the Gel Moisturiser. Tender coconut water in the Face Mist. Read the full ingredient list on each product page before you buy.

COLLECTION 1: DRY SKIN

Intro
For skin that feels tight or looks flaky. Start with the cream if the dryness is on your face. Choose the body butter if it is on your arms, elbows and legs.

Product tiles
Rich Coconut Cream 50 g: Rich face cream for tight, dry cheeks, made with virgin coconut oil
Coconut Body Butter 200 g: Shea butter body care for dry arms, elbows and legs

COLLECTION 2: DULL SKIN

Intro
For skin that looks dull. Start with the face wash, which suits every day. Add the scrub once your skin needs more than a wash.

Product tiles
Turmeric Face Scrub 75 g: For a deeper polish when skin looks tired
Coconut Milk Face Wash 100 ml: Your everyday cleanse, made with coconut milk

COLLECTION 3: OILY OR STICKY SKIN

Intro
For skin that turns oily or sticky in humid weather. Start with the aloe gel if creams feel too heavy. Keep the mist in your bag for a midday refresh.

Product tiles
Aloe Gel Moisturiser 50 g: A light gel made with aloe vera, for humid days
Coconut Water Face Mist 100 ml: A mist for sticky afternoons, made with tender coconut water

UPLOAD NOTE
Product names and pack sizes above must match the listing titles exactly. Use the same names on the Shopify site and in ads.

# GST registration for Etsy and Amazon sellers in Rajasthan: 8 questions answered

If you sell handmade goods from home in Rajasthan on Amazon or Etsy, GST advice reaches you in three conflicting versions. This page answers the eight questions home-based craft sellers ask us most, for sellers doing Rs 5-40 lakh a year. The short answer: if any order leaves Rajasthan, for another state or another country, you need a GST number, with one narrow exception for notified handicrafts (answer 2). Your home can be your place of business.

## Ghar ke address pe GST mil jayega?

Yes. You can register GST at your home and list it as your place of business, whether you own the flat or rent it. An officer may visit to check, so keep the address documents ready.

Own home: the latest electricity bill or property-tax receipt. Rented home: the rent agreement, the landlord's consent letter and an electricity bill. A family member's home: their consent letter and an electricity bill. The address then prints on every invoice, so if you move your workshop, amend the registration instead of leaving the old address on the portal.

## Etsy pe bahar bechne ke liye GST chahiye?

Yes, in almost every case. Selling to a buyer abroad is an inter-state supply under Section 7(5) of the IGST Act. Anyone making an inter-state supply of goods must register under Section 24 of the CGST Act, whatever the turnover.

The one exception is notified handicraft goods: a seller whose inter-state supplies of such goods stay within Rs 20 lakh a year can skip registration under Notification 3/2018-Integrated Tax, with conditions. Check your product against its list. Even then, only a registered seller can file a Letter of Undertaking (LUT), the document that lets you export without paying IGST. You file it online in Form GST RFD-11, once for each financial year. Keep the courier or postal export documents and the payment proof for every order.

## Amazon pe bechna hai, turnover kam hai, phir bhi GST lena padega?

Usually yes. Section 24(ix) of the CGST Act requires every seller who supplies goods through an e-commerce marketplace to register, whatever the turnover. A seller under Rs 40 lakh a year can skip it only if every order stays inside one state.

Notification 34/2023-Central Tax, in force since 1 October 2023, sets the conditions. Goods only, sold through the marketplace in a single state. Turnover within the state's limit, which is Rs 40 lakh for goods in Rajasthan. And an enrolment number from the GST portal before the first sale. Most Amazon sellers ship across India, and one order to another state ends the exemption.

## GST number aane mein kitne din lagte hain?

About 7 working days if your Aadhaar authentication is done and the officer has no query. If the portal flags the application for physical verification, or Aadhaar authentication is not done, it can take up to 30 days.

If the officer needs more, you get a notice in Form GST REG-03 and have 7 working days to reply in Form GST REG-04. The officer then has 7 working days to decide. Send the exact documents asked for, in one reply. A missed date can end in rejection (Form GST REG-05). In the case below, an officer's visit took the GSTIN to 19 days.

## Composition scheme le sakte hain ya marketplace pe bechne se nahi milti?

Not if any order goes to another state or abroad, because a composition taxpayer cannot make inter-state supplies. Since 1 October 2023, composition sellers may sell goods through a marketplace, but only inside their own state.

Composition means paying a flat 1% of turnover instead of regular GST. The price is that you cannot charge GST to buyers, cannot claim credit on fabric, dye or packing, and issue a bill of supply, not a tax invoice. That is why craft sellers who ship across India or abroad take the regular scheme. If you sell only inside Rajasthan, ask us before choosing: 1% looks cheap until you lose the input credit.

## Amazon jo TCS kaat leta hai, uska hisaab kaise rakhna hai?

TCS is tax collected at source. Amazon deducts 0.5% of your net taxable sales (sales minus returns) and deposits it for you. It lands in your electronic cash ledger once Amazon files its monthly statement, and you use it to pay your GST.

Each month, match three things: your settlement statement, the TCS shown on your GST portal, and your cash ledger. If a figure differs, raise it with the marketplace before you file. Illustration, not a client's figures: net taxable sales of Rs 4,00,000 mean TCS of Rs 2,000. If your GST on those sales is Rs 20,000, you pay Rs 18,000 yourself and the TCS covers the rest.

## Return har mahine bharna padta hai ya quarter mein?

Monthly by default. If your turnover in the last financial year was up to Rs 5 crore, you can choose the QRMP scheme: file returns every quarter, but pay tax every month. Either way, file even when you had no sales.

Under QRMP you pay each month's tax by challan (Form GST PMT-06) by the 25th, and file GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B for the quarter. Amazon reports your sales to the department in its own monthly statement, so your return must match its figures. A mismatch can bring a notice. Late filing costs a daily fee, plus interest on any tax paid late.

## Officer verification ke liye ghar aaye toh kya dikhana hai?

The same documents you uploaded: PAN, Aadhaar and your address proof. For a rented flat, keep the rent agreement, the landlord's consent letter and an electricity bill ready on the table. The officer checks that a business really runs from that address.

A visit happens when the portal flags an application or an officer decides to verify. It is routine, not a penalty. Keep your stock, packing table and order records in view, so the officer sees a working business and not just a flat.

## From our files: a Jaipur cushion-cover seller

A home-based block-print cushion-cover seller in Jaipur, turnover Rs 28 lakh a year, about Rs 9 lakh of it Etsy orders to the US and UK. She applied for registration listing her rented flat as her place of business. An officer's verification visit followed. He asked for the rent agreement, the landlord's consent letter and an electricity bill. Her GSTIN came 19 days after she applied. We filed her LUT 6 days after the GSTIN, so her Etsy orders could ship without IGST. Her first return went in on time, and she has had no notice since. Anonymised case.

Two lessons: gather the three address documents before you apply, and file the LUT within days of getting the GSTIN.

## Not sure which of these applies to you?

Book a Rs 999 registration consult. We look at your products, your marketplaces and your turnover, and tell you which registration route fits. [Booking link]

Written by [author name], CA, [firm name], Jaipur. Reviewed by [reviewer name], CA, membership no. [number]. Last updated 13 October 2026.

# "The first order was for learning, not earning": KaarigarKart's founder on winning US boutique buyers

In March 2024, a boutique owner in Portland, Oregon found KaarigarKart's block-print tablecloths on Instagram, paid for a sample, then ordered 40 pieces worth Rs 92,000. Sanjana Chaudhary, who founded the Jaipur handicraft export marketplace, kept 11% of that order. Since then she has changed how she quotes, how she invoices and how she credits the people who make the product, and she now earns 24% on repeat orders. For Indian SME exporters weighing a first US quote, her numbers are the useful part, including the awkward ones. We asked her how she found buyers, what the first order really cost and what she would tell the next exporter. The figures are her own and were not independently audited. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. Sanjana has reviewed it for factual accuracy only.

## Finding the buyer

**Where did your first US order come from?**

A boutique owner in Portland, Oregon found our block-print tablecloths on Instagram. [This was in March 2024.]

**Did the Portland boutique order straight away?**

She paid for a sample first, and then ordered 40 pieces worth Rs 92,000. [That is Rs 2,300 a tablecloth.]

**Did you also go looking for buyers, or did you wait for them to find you?**

I did not wait to be found. I sent 300 Instagram DMs to boutique owners; 14 replied, and 3 became orders. [Fourteen replies from 300 messages is under 5%. Three orders is 1%, or about one in five replies. That is one account's outreach, not a benchmark.]

## Pricing the first order

**Commission, courier and customs came out of that Rs 92,000. What was left?**

The marketplace commission is 18%. Courier and customs paperwork took another 14%. My margin on that first order was 11%; on repeat orders it is 24%. [On Rs 92,000, and assuming each percentage applies to the order value, that is Rs 16,560 in commission, Rs 12,880 in courier and customs, and Rs 10,120 of margin. Out of every Rs 100, Rs 57 remained for everything else, including making the tablecloths.]

**Where did the quote go wrong?**

I quoted FOB prices, but the buyer wanted delivered prices. So I absorbed Rs 6,200 of freight myself, and that sits inside the 14%. [FOB means free on board: the seller's price ends when the goods are loaded, and the buyer pays freight from there. A delivered price includes freight to the buyer's door. Strictly, FOB describes sea freight; for air shipments the usual term is FCA. Rs 6,200 is about 6.7% of the order.]

**What did you change afterwards?**

After that freight lesson, we changed how we quote. Now we quote delivered prices, every time. The HS code, 6302, goes on every invoice. [Whether a delivered price also covers import duty depends on the Incoterm agreed: DAP leaves duty with the buyer, DDP puts it on the seller. The HS code is the international system customs uses to classify goods; heading 6302 covers bed, table, toilet and kitchen linen, which includes tablecloths. Countries add digits beyond the sixth, so confirm the full code for block-print cotton tablecloths with a customs broker.]

**Eleven percent on a Rs 92,000 order is thin. Why take it?**

Pehla order kamaane ka nahi, seekhne ka tha [the first order was for learning, not earning]. The margin on it was thin, and what I learned from it is what the repeat orders run on.

## Advice and what comes next

**What would you tell an exporter before their first order?**

My advice is simple. Send a paid sample before the first order. That is exactly how the Portland order began for us.

**What is the next goal?**

I want 10 boutiques reordering twice a year. Repeat orders are where the 24% margin is, so that is what I am building towards. [Ten boutiques reordering twice a year is 20 reorders. If each is the size of the first order, 24% is about Rs 22,080 a reorder, against Rs 10,120 at 11%.]

**What changed on your product pages?**

Kaarigar ka naam sabse bada brand hai [the artisan's name is the biggest brand]. So every product page now names the block-printer who made that piece.

Four things to copy this week

1. Send a paid sample before you quote a first order. It is how her Rs 92,000 order began.
2. Quote delivered prices, with freight inside the price, and print the HS code on every invoice. Her Rs 6,200 freight surprise came from the one thing the quote left out.
3. Track margin on first orders and repeat orders separately. Her own gap is 11% against 24%, and the second figure is the one she is building the business on.
4. Put the maker's name on the product page, as she does for every block-printer.

Sanjana Chaudhary is the founder of KaarigarKart, a Jaipur handicraft export marketplace that sells block-print textiles to boutique buyers in the US. Find her at [website or Instagram handle].

Selling to US buyers, or planning to? Register for the [newsletter name] exporter webinar on [date and time]: [registration link].
samples.writer_note: Every answer is her own transcript excerpt verbatim; excerpts are split or paired only where the context is the same, and nothing in her voice is added. Both Hindi phrases stay, with bracketed translations. Square-bracket editor's notes add only arithmetic from her figures (Rs 2,300 a piece; Rs 16,560, 12,880 and 10,120 on Rs 92,000 if each percentage is of order value, stated in the text; Rs 6,200 is 6.7%; Rs 22,080 on a reorder the size of the first) and public facts (FOB/FCA, Incoterms DAP/DDP, HS heading 6302). The freight contradiction is fixed in the brief and in the piece (Rs 6,200 inside the 14%). 10 exchanges, every question shorter than its answer, the hard margin question is exchange 7 and follows the freight story. Length: 859 words against the brief's 900-1,200 (the card's 700 minimum is met). Why short: her nine excerpts hold about 210 words and I would not invent answers; her words run 12-28 per answer, 40-90 with the bracketed notes. Placeholders: website or handle, newsletter name, webinar date and link.

META AD COPY: millet snack trial pack (Instagram and Facebook feed)

VARIANT 1: the 7 am tiffin question
Angle note (working, not published): pain. Cold, problem-aware parents in metros. Tests whether the daily tiffin scene pulls more clicks than label proof or price.
Primary text, visible opening: 7 baje tiffin ka sawaal: aaj kya rakhein? Baked jowar-ragi puffs, 6 packs, Rs 299, free shipping.
Primary text, body: Sandwich again? Each 25 g pack is small enough for the tiffin box, and the trial comes in three flavours: masala, tomato and plain. Get the trial pack and test it on Monday's tiffin.
Headline: Millet puffs for the tiffin
Description: Pune millet-snack brand.
CTA button: Shop Now

VARIANT 2: read the label
Angle note (working, not published): proof. Same parents, label readers who do not know the brand. Tests whether the printed ingredient list earns more trust than the pain hook.
Primary text, visible opening: Label padhne ki aadat hai? Jowar 60%, ragi 25%, rice bran oil, rock salt, spices. No maida, no palm oil. Trial pack Rs 299.
Primary text, body: That is the full list, exactly as printed on the pack. Baked puffs in masala, tomato and plain, six 25 g packs, shipped free. Get the trial pack and read the label for yourself.
Headline: Jowar, ragi, no maida
Description: 6 x 25 g packs in 3 flavours.
CTA button: Learn More

VARIANT 3: the trial price
Angle note (working, not published): offer. Most-aware viewers who want a low-risk first order. Tests the trial price and free shipping against the other two angles.
Primary text, visible opening: Rs 299, free shipping: 6 packs of baked jowar-ragi puffs in masala, tomato and plain. Try before you stock up.
Primary text, body: That is under Rs 50 a pack, with all three flavours in the box. Pehle try karo, phir stock karo. Get the trial pack and pick a favourite before you order more.
Headline: Rs 299 trial, free shipping
Description: Free shipping on the trial pack.
CTA button: Shop Now
samples.writer_note: Uses the product facts now in the brief: baked jowar-ragi puffs in masala, tomato and plain, the printed ingredient list (variant 2 opening is the list itself) and 6 x 25 g packs; every opening names the product, so no variant leaves the reader asking what it is. No placeholders, no health, taste or nutrition claim; 'no maida, no palm oil' is the printed fact. 'Under Rs 50 a pack' is Rs 299 / 6 = Rs 49.83. Bodies add a reason each (tiffin fit and flavours; the label as the offer; unit price and low commitment) instead of repeating Rs 299. Openings 97, 123 and 110 characters (limit 125); headlines 27, 21 and 27 (Facebook feed limit 27); descriptions differ; CTA buttons Shop Now, Learn More, Shop Now, all to the trial-pack page. The landing page must show the same price, free shipping, pack contents, flavours and ingredient list; the percentages are demo facts and must match the real pack. Hindi lines use gender-neutral forms (rakhein, padhne ki aadat hai, karo).

samples.brief: Topic: TOPICS[1] = a Pune cloud-kitchen brand launching a high-protein thali. Surface: first line of an Instagram feed ad (primary text, plat:meta_ads field 'primary text, Instagram feed', 125 characters recommended). Demo facts the kitchen would confirm (fictional): a vegetarian thali of dal, paneer bhurji, jowar roti, curd and salad; weekday delivery to Baner, Aundh and Kothrud; launch on Monday 19 October 2026. No body, weight or health outcome, no number in any hook (none is supplied), no staged customer result: each hook contrasts a different old lunch situation with what the box now holds, so both states are concrete and the body can show the thali. Five different contrasts, not one idea five times; at least one in Hinglish.
samples.text:
1. Before: a biscuit packet between meetings. After: dal, paneer bhurji, jowar roti, curd and salad in one box.
   Template: Before: [old way]. After: [new way].
2. A full thali on your desk at lunch. A week ago it was the canteen queue. Here's what changed.
   Template: [After state]. [Time] ago it looked like this. Here's what changed.
3. Pehle: Sunday ko sabzi kaato, dabbe bharo. Ab: dopahar ko thali ka dabba khol lo. Farak sirf Sunday ke meal-prep ka hai.
   Template: Pehle: [before]. Ab: [after]. Farak sirf [one change] ka hai.
4. From 'what's for lunch?' in the group chat to a full thali at your desk: one order, no cooking.
   Template: From [before metric] to [after metric]: [method in 3-5 words]. (states instead of metrics: no real figure exists, and the card bans invented numbers)
5. Before: a tiffin packed at 7 am. After: a thali delivered to Baner, Aundh or Kothrud for lunch.
   Template: Before: [old way]. After: [new way].
samples.writer_note: Earlier fault ('all five are one idea: plain dal-chawal then a [N]g protein thali', a '[Time] ago' with no time, a circular 'ek thali ka farak') addressed: five different old-lunch scenes (a biscuit packet between meetings, the canteen queue, Sunday meal-prep, the group-chat 'what's for lunch?', the 7 am tiffin), no protein grams or any other number, and in the Hinglish line the 'one change' is the Sunday meal-prep itself. Four templates exist for five hooks, so Before/After is used twice, on different contrasts. Hook 4 swaps the template's metrics for states, which the card allows when no real figure exists. 'A week ago' and '7 am' are scene-setting, not claims about a customer. Longest hook is 109 characters. Menu and areas are demo facts in the brief.

samples.brief: Topic: TOPICS[1] = a Pune cloud-kitchen brand launching a high-protein thali. Surface: launch email subject line to the kitchen's subscriber list (plat:email_subject_line; fields subject line chars+words, punctuation marks, emojis: 60 chars, 9 words, 3 punctuation), chosen over Pinterest because the reader is a customer who will order. It is a done-for-you product, so per the card the hooks never quantify the ordering (no taps, steps or order minutes) and give no delivery time; each hook sizes or names a different effort the reader skips: Sunday prep hours, packing a tiffin, minutes at the stove, the grocery list, washing up. Each [N] is a figure the kitchen takes from its own subscriber survey (none is supplied, so none is invented). No nutrition number, price or menu item. 'Quick' and 'easy' are never stacked in one line; at least one in Hinglish.
samples.text:
1. The lazy way to lunch: no [N]-hour Sunday prep
   Template: The [lazy / quick] way to [result] ([time]). ([time] filled with the effort skipped, not the ordering)
2. A quick way to lunch without packing a tiffin
   Template: Here's a quick way to [task] without [usual hassle].
3. Easy lunch: skip the [N] minutes at the stove
   Template: [Result] the easy way: [N] steps, [time] total. (steps swapped for the minutes skipped: counting the ordering steps is what the card now forbids)
4. A quick way to plan lunch: no grocery list
   Template: Here's a quick way to [task] without [usual hassle].
5. Roz ka lunch, bina bartan dhoye, bina jhanjhat ke
   Template: [Task] sirf [N] minute mein, bina [hassle] ke. ('sirf [N] minute mein' dropped: it reads as a delivery time)
samples.writer_note: Earlier fault (three of five measured the ordering, 'sirf [N] minute mein' read as delivery time, #2 was broken English) addressed: nothing counts taps, steps or order minutes; the effort named is Sunday prep, tiffin, stove time, the grocery list and washing up, two of them sized with a kitchen-supplied [N]. The Hinglish line drops the minutes clause for that reason and says so. The 'using only [tool]' template is not used: for a delivered meal it would only restate the ordering. 'Quick' appears in hooks 2 and 4 and 'easy' in hook 3, never together. Word counts 9, 9, 9, 9, 9; longest 49 characters.

samples.brief: Topic: TOPICS[6] = a monsoon skincare range from an Ayurvedic D2C brand. Surface: Meta (Instagram feed) image ad with a rain-and-product image: the punchy line is the ad headline (plat:meta_ads, field 'headline, Instagram feed', 40 chars) and the subhead is the primary text (field 'primary text, Instagram feed', 125 chars); the image and both texts always appear together. No cure or result word (no 'cured', 'clear', 'guaranteed'), no price, ingredient list or certification invented. Each line is a different concrete monsoon moment the image completes, and each subhead carries that moment instead of restating the product; at least one in Hinglish.
samples.text:
1. Local train.  Subhead: Sticky by the second station. Ayurvedic monsoon skincare for the commute. See the range.
   Template: [One concrete noun].  Subhead: [specific promise, place, price].
2. Wear the rain.  Subhead: Sweat under the helmet strap, drizzle on the way back. An Ayurvedic range for monsoon rides. Shop now.
   Template: [Verb] [object].  Subhead: [who it is for and how].
3. Chipchipahat.  Subhead: Barish ke din, chipchipi si skin. Ayurvedic monsoon range, in dinon ke liye. Dekhiye.
   Template: [Hindi word or phrase].  Subhead: [what to do, where].
4. Wet chappals.  Subhead: Wet chappals, sticky arms, a bus that is late. Ayurvedic monsoon skincare for days like this. See the range.
   Template: [One concrete noun].  Subhead: [specific promise, place, price].
5. Pasina.  Subhead: Barish mein bhi pasina aata hai. Ayurvedic monsoon range, in dinon ke liye. Dekhiye.
   Template: [Hindi word or phrase].  Subhead: [what to do, where].
samples.writer_note: Earlier fault ('Humid. Ayurveda.' is the abstract pair the card bans, 'Switch routines.' says nothing, all five subheads restate 'Ayurvedic skincare for humid days') addressed: every headline is a concrete noun, an image-ready verb phrase or a Hindi sensory word (local train, wear the rain, chipchipahat = stickiness, wet chappals, pasina = sweat), and every subhead carries a felt moment (sticky by the second station, sweat under the helmet strap, wet chappals and a late bus) with no product claim beyond 'Ayurvedic monsoon range'. The [adjective]. [noun]. template is not used on purpose: it needs a documented proof line and the topic supplies none, so a proof slot would repeat the old fault; its place is taken by a second concrete-noun line and a second Hindi line. Same topic and surface as the earlier sample. Headlines 12-14 characters; subheads 84-108 characters.

samples.brief: Topic: TOPICS[2] = an AI tool that turns Hindi voice notes into meeting minutes (changed from the one-village story, which has a single case and so cannot carry this hook; this topic has a real crowd). Demo proof facts (fictional; the client replaces them with substantiated figures and keeps the source file): 4.6 stars from 3,870 Google Play reviews as of 1 October 2026; 1,140 Indian teams used the app in September 2026, including 212 CA firms, 38 of them in Jaipur. Surface: first line of a Meta (Instagram and Facebook feed) ad, primary text (plat:meta_ads, field 'primary text, Instagram feed', 125 characters recommended); audience: Indian SME owners and CA-firm partners. Every number carries its unit and time window, none is rounded up, and no crowd is claimed beyond these facts; one hook per card template, at least one in Hinglish.
samples.text:
1. 1,140 Indian teams used this app in September 2026 to turn Hindi voice notes into meeting minutes.
   Template: [Number] [peer group] [use / switched to] [product] for [result].
2. Here's a method that helped 212 CA firms in India turn Hindi voice notes into minutes in September 2026.
   Template: Here's a method that is helping [group] [result]. (past tense, because the count is a closed month)
3. Join the 3,870 people who reviewed this app on Google Play (4.6 stars). Hindi voice note in, minutes out.
   Template: Join [number] [group] who [action] every [period]. (the action is the review; the period is the 1 October 2026 snapshot)
4. CA firms across India use this to turn Hindi voice notes into meeting minutes. See how it works.
   Template: [Recognisable peer group] [uses] this to [result].
5. Jaipur ke 38 CA firms ye already use kar rahe hain: Hindi voice note se meeting minutes.
   Template: [City] ke [number] [group] ye already use kar rahe hain.
samples.writer_note: Judge's fault was test design (one village is one case, not a crowd), so the topic is TOPICS[2] with demo proof facts stated in the brief; they are fictional and the client must replace them with figures it can document (the substantiation file the card's technique asks for: claim, source, date). One hook per card template, each using a different fact: 1,140 teams (September 2026), 212 CA firms (September 2026), 3,870 reviews and 4.6 stars (Google Play, 1 October 2026), no number for the peer-group line, 38 Jaipur CA firms for the Hinglish line. Nothing is rounded up, there is no live counter, and no 'X people viewing' line. Hook 3 reads the 4.6 as the average of the reviews, not a score each reviewer gave. 'This app' stands in for the unnamed product.
